extracted.intended_audience: educated British public, political leaders, and readers concerned with the French Revolution and the preservation of British institutions
extracted.subtask_description: A political essay arguing for the preservation of Britain’s established institutions (church, monarchy, aristocracy, and measured democracy) and condemning radical subversion such as the French revolutionary confiscation of church property. Intended to persuade readers of the prudence and moral necessity of these establishments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion as the basis of civil society
rubrics_metrics.description: We know, and, what is better, we feel inwardly, that religion is the basis of civil society, and the source of all good, and of all comfort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religion supplies moral foundations and civic consolation; the vast majority of the people prefer religion to impiety, and it should not be discarded or replaced by atheism or other destructive doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve established institutions in their existing degree
rubrics_metrics.description: We are resolved to keep an established church, an established monarchy, an established aristocracy, and an established democracy, each in the degree it exists, and in no greater.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain the existing mixed constitution and social establishments rather than expanding or abolishing them; balance of the different estates should be respected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not call in atheism to reform religion
rubrics_metrics.description: If our religious tenets should ever want a further elucidation, we shall not call on Atheism to explain them. We shall not light up our temple from that unhallowed fire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reform or clarification of religion must not be sought by adopting the enemies or subverters of religion; using radical anti-religious philosophies to 'cleanse' religion is inadmissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consecration of the state by a religious establishment
rubrics_metrics.description: This consecration is made, that all who administer in the government of men, in which they stand in the person of God Himself, should have high and worthy notions of their function and destination; that their hope should be full of immortality...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A state religious establishment elevates the sense of duty among officeholders, encouraging permanence of moral purpose rather than transient or paltry aims; public sanctification of offices helps preserve virtue in governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion impresses accountability on those in power
rubrics_metrics.description: All persons possessing any portion of power ought to be strongly and awfully impressed with an idea that they act in trust, and that they are to account for their conduct in that trust to the one great Master, Author, and Founder of society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious belief and institutions foster an internal check on abuse of power; without such impressions, rulers and officeholders are more likely to pursue self-interest and arbitrary domination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on unchecked democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: A perfect democracy is therefore the most shameless thing in the world. As it is the most shameless, it is also the most fearless... The people at large never ought [to be the subject of punishment by any human hand].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns that absolute popular sovereignty without restraints leads to shamelessness, impunity, and poor moral judgment; the people’s will is not the sole standard of right and wrong and must be tempered by institutions and principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach reforms cautiously; avoid subversion as a method of reformation
rubrics_metrics.description: He should never dream of beginning its reformation by its subversion; that he should approach to the faults of the state as to the wounds of a father, with pious awe and trembling solicitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reformers ought to repair and improve institutions conservatively and respectfully rather than seek total overthrow; radical subversion risks destroying the chain and continuity of the commonwealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Society as an intergenerational contract
rubrics_metrics.description: Society is, indeed, a contract... It is a partnership in all science, a partnership in all art, a partnership in every virtue and in all perfection... between those who are living, those who are dead, and those who are to be born.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The state should be treated as a long-term trust binding past, present, and future generations; this justifies restraint on facile dissolution or wholesale alteration of institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value continuity and study of jurisprudence
rubrics_metrics.description: The science of jurisprudence... is the collected reason of ages... would be no longer studied. Personal self-sufficiency and arrogance... would usurp the tribunal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stable laws and respect for legal tradition are essential for education, property, honor, and the arts; frequent, radical changes undermine legal learning and social continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education should be integrated with the Church and its clergy
rubrics_metrics.description: Our education is in a manner wholly in the hands of ecclesiastics, and in all stages from infancy to manhood... three fourths of those who go abroad with our young nobility and gentlemen are ecclesiastics... With them... they most commonly keep up a close connection through life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clerical involvement in education binds elites to the Church and preserves religious influence and moral instruction across classes; education grounded in tradition aids improvement without destroying the past.

rubrics_metrics.name: Church estates should be independent property, not state pensions
rubrics_metrics.description: They certainly never have suffered, and never will suffer, the fixed estate of the Church to be converted into a pension, to depend on the Treasury... The people of England think that they have constitutional motives, as well as religious, against any project of turning their independent clergy into ecclesiastical pensioners of state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Church revenues should be secure and independent so clergy do not become state pensioners (which would endanger liberty) nor wholly subject to crown influence; stability of provision preserves independence and public trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public ceremonial and ornament of religion as public good
rubrics_metrics.description: This our corporate fealty and homage... should be performed, as all public, solemn acts are performed, in buildings, in music, in decoration, in speech, in the dignity of persons... It is the public ornament. It is the public consolation. It nourishes the public hope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public worship, ceremony, and visible religious monuments reinforce social cohesion, give dignity to the poor, and serve as public consolation and moral education; such expenditures are a legitimate public use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condemn confiscation of church property
rubrics_metrics.description: There is not _one_ public man in this kingdom... who does not reprobate the dishonest, perfidious, and cruel confiscation which the National Assembly has been compelled to make of that property which it was their first duty to protect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seizure and proscription of ecclesiastical property (as in the French revolutionary example) are unjust, cruel, and politically destructive; protecting property rights of church estates preserves public order and sympathy for religion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance public provision with voluntary charity
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole Church revenue is not always employed, and to every shilling, in charity; nor perhaps ought it; but something is generally so employed. It is better to cherish virtue and humanity, by leaving much to free will, even with some loss to the object...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While church wealth should serve charitable ends, some discretionary private use and voluntary philanthropy are valuable; attempting to convert all church revenue into state-directed charity risks undermining voluntarism and virtue.
